title: Containers: Choosing One, and What It Costs

questions.question: Which container should be the default choice?
options: std::vector, because contiguous memory is what processors are fast at
std::map, because lookup is logarithmic
std::unordered_map, because lookup is constant
std::list, because inserting anywhere is cheap
questions.explanation: Reading one element pulls its neighbours into cache, so scanning a vector routinely beats a structure that scatters elements, even for lookup at small sizes.

questions.question: Why is a vector's amortised constant push a problem in a control loop?
options: The individual push that reallocates is not constant, and it happens at a moment the loop did not choose
Because push_back is slow in general
Because vectors cannot hold more than a few thousand elements
Because the amortised cost grows with size
questions.explanation: Amortised constant is a statement about the average. A loop with a deadline cares about the worst case, and the worst case arrives on a schedule set by history.

questions.question: What happens to a reference into a vector when the vector reallocates?
options: It dangles, and using it is undefined behaviour with no warning
It is updated to point at the new location
The compiler refuses to compile such code
Nothing, references into vectors are always stable
questions.explanation: It works until the push happens to reallocate, which depends on the capacity, which depends on how many elements arrived earlier. That is why it surfaces late.

questions.question: Why does the reference use std::map rather than std::unordered_map for the latest reading?
options: names() wants sorted order, and a map provides it for free
Because unordered_map cannot hold strings
Because map lookup is faster
Because unordered_map does not allow assignment
questions.explanation: Getting the ordering from the container beats sorting on every call. An unordered_map would also give an order that can change between runs, which makes output hard to compare.

questions.question: In a full ring buffer, where is the oldest entry?
options: At the position about to be overwritten next
Always at index zero
At the position written most recently
At the midpoint of the buffer
questions.explanation: Once the buffer has wrapped, the write position and the oldest entry are the same slot. Assuming index zero produces output that is correct only until the first wrap.

questions.question: What does complexity notation not tell you?
options: How fast something actually is on real hardware
How the cost grows with size
Whether an operation is constant time
The worst case behaviour
questions.explanation: A logarithmic lookup that follows pointers to scattered nodes can lose to a linear scan of memory already in cache. Start with a vector and change when a measurement says to.
